{{Short description|Mathematical function}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Witten zeta function''', is a function associated to a [[root system]] that encodes the degrees of the [[irreducible representation]]s of the corresponding [[Lie group]]. These zeta functions were introduced by [[Don Zagier]] who named them after [[Edward Witten]]'s study of their special values (among other things).<ref>{{Citation|last=Zagier|first=Don|date=1994|pages=497–512|publisher=Birkhäuser Basel|doi=10.1007/978-3-0348-9112-7_23|isbn=9783034899123|chapter=Values of Zeta Functions and Their Applications|title=First European Congress of Mathematics Paris, July 6–10, 1992}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Witten|first=Edward|date=October 1991|title=On quantum gauge theories in two dimensions|journal=[[Communications in Mathematical Physics]]|volume=141|issue=1|pages=153–209|doi=10.1007/bf02100009|bibcode=1991CMaPh.141..153W |s2cid=121994550 |issn=0010-3616|url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.cmp/1104248198 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Note that in,<ref name=":0" /> Witten zeta functions do not appear as explicit objects in their own right.

==Definition==
If <math>G</math> is a compact semisimple Lie group, the associated Witten zeta function is (the meromorphic continuation of) the series  
:<math>\zeta_G(s)=\sum_\rho\frac{1}{(\dim\rho)^s},</math>

where the sum is over equivalence classes of irreducible representations of <math>G</math>.

In the case where <math>G</math> is connected and simply connected, the correspondence between representations of <math>G</math> and of its Lie algebra, together with the Weyl dimension formula, implies that <math>\zeta_G(s)</math> can be written as

:<math>\sum_{m_1,\dots,m_r>0}\prod_{\alpha\in \Phi^+}\frac{1}{\langle\alpha^\lor, m_1\lambda_1+\cdots+m_r\lambda_r\rangle^{s}},</math>

where <math>\Phi^+</math> denotes the set of positive roots, <math>\{\lambda_i\}</math> is a set of simple roots and <math>r</math> is the rank.

== Examples ==

* <math>\zeta_{SU(2)}(s)=\zeta(s)</math>, the [[Riemann zeta function]].
* <math>\zeta_{SU(3)}(s)=\sum_{x=1}^{\infty}\sum_{y=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(xy(x+y)/2)^s}.</math>

== Abscissa of convergence ==
If <math>G</math> is simple and simply connected, the abscissa of convergence of <math>\zeta_G(s)</math> is <math>r/\kappa</math>, where <math>r</math> is the rank and <math>\kappa=|\Phi^{+}|</math>. This is a theorem due to Alex Lubotzky and Michael Larsen.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Larsen|first1=Michael|last2=Lubotzky|first2=Alexander|year=2008|title=Representation growth of linear groups|journal=[[Journal of the European Mathematical Society]]|volume=10|issue=2|pages=351–390|doi=10.4171/JEMS/113|issn=1435-9855|arxiv=math/0607369|s2cid=9322647 }}</ref> A new proof is given by Jokke Häsä and Alexander Stasinski 
<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Häsä |first1=Jokke |last2=Stasinski |first2=Alexander |title=Representation growth of compact linear groups |journal=[[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]] |date=2019 |volume=372 |issue=2 |pages=925–980 |doi=10.1090/tran/7618|doi-access=free |arxiv=1710.09112 }}</ref> 
which yields a more general result, namely it gives an explicit value (in terms of simple combinatorics) of the abscissa of convergence of any "Mellin zeta function" of the form

<math>\sum_{x_1,\dots,x_r=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{P(x_1,\dots,x_r)^s},</math>

where <math>P(x_1,\dots,x_r)</math> is a product of linear polynomials with non-negative real coefficients.

== Singularities and values of the Witten zeta function associated to SU(3) ==
<math>\zeta_{SU(3)}</math> is absolutely convergent in <math>\{ s \in \mathbb{C}, \Re(s)>2/3 \}</math>, and it can be extended meromorphically in <math>\mathbb{C}</math>. Its singularities are in <math> \Bigl\{ \frac{2}{3} \Bigr\} \cup \Bigl\{ \frac{1}{2}-k, k \in \mathbb{N}  \Bigr\},</math> and all of those singularities are simple poles.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Romik |first=Dan |date=2017 |title=On the number of $n$-dimensional representations of $\operatorname{SU}(3)$, the Bernoulli numbers, and the Witten zeta function |url=http://www.impan.pl/get/doi/10.4064/aa8455-3-2017 |journal=Acta Arithmetica |language=en |volume=180 |issue=2 |pages=111–159 |doi=10.4064/aa8455-3-2017 |issn=0065-1036|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In particular, the values of <math>\zeta_{SU(3)}(s)</math> are well defined at all integers, and have been computed by Kazuhiro Onodera.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Onodera |first=Kazuhiro |date=2014 |title=A functional relation for Tornheim's double zeta functions |url=http://journals.impan.pl/cgi-bin/doi?aa162-4-2 |journal=Acta Arithmetica |language=en |volume=162 |issue=4 |pages=337–354 |doi=10.4064/aa162-4-2 |arxiv=1211.1480 |s2cid=119636956 |issn=0065-1036}}</ref>

At <math>s=0</math>, we have <math>\zeta_{SU(3)}(0) = \frac{1}{3},</math> and <math>\zeta_{SU(3)}'(0)=\log(2^{4/3}\pi).</math>

Let <math>a \in \mathbb{N}^*</math> be a positive [[integer]]. We have

<math>\zeta_{SU(3)}(a)=\frac{2^{a+2}}{1+(-1)^a 2} \sum_{k=0}^{[a/2]} {2a-2k-1 \choose a-1} \zeta(2k) \zeta(3a-k).</math>

If a is odd, then <math>\zeta_{SU(3)}</math> has a simple zero at <math>s=-a,</math> and

<math>\zeta_{SU(3)}'(-a)=\frac{2^{-a+1} (a!)^2}{(2a+1)!} \zeta'(-3a-1) + 2^{-a+2} \sum_{k=0}^{(a-1)/2} {a \choose 2k} \zeta(-a-2k) \zeta'(-2a+2k).</math>

If a is even, then <math>\zeta_{SU(3)}</math> has a zero of order <math>2</math> at <math>s=-a,</math> and

<math>\zeta_{SU(3)}''(-a)=2^{-a+2}\sum_{k=0}^{a/2} {a \choose 2k} \zeta'(-a-2k)\zeta'(-2a+2k).</math>
